title: Lightest Heaviest of k Runs
statement:
You get an array nums of non-negative integers and a number k. Cut the array into exactly k non-empty contiguous runs, keeping the original order. The cost of a cut is the sum of its heaviest run.

Return the smallest cost you can reach.

examples.why: [4, 1, 5] | [2, 6] has run sums 10 and 8. Every other cut has a run of 12 or 13.
Each value is its own run. k equal to the length forces this.
[1] | [9] | [1, 1, 1, 1]. The total split three ways would be under 5, but no run can weigh less than the 9 inside it.

hints: Turn the question around. If someone hands you a limit L, can you quickly tell whether the array can be cut into at most k runs, none heavier than L?
For a fixed limit, greedy works: keep extending the current run until the next value would push it past L, then start a new run. Fewer runs than k is fine, since a run can always be split further.
The test 'possible with limit L' is false for small L and true from some point on. Binary search L between max(nums) and sum(nums).

explain.intuition:
Finding the best cut directly is hard. Checking a proposed answer is easy: given a limit L, walk the array and start a new run only when the next value would overflow L. That greedy uses the fewest runs possible, because packing as much as you can into each run never leaves you worse off later. If it needs at most k runs, L is achievable (split any run further to reach exactly k; the max cannot grow).

Achievable limits form a block: once some L works, every larger one works too. So binary search on L between the heaviest single value (no run can be lighter) and the total (one run). It is the same idea as finding the narrowest column width that fits text into a fixed number of lines.
steps: For a candidate mid, count runs greedily: add values to the current run, and when the next value would exceed mid, start a new run with it.
If the count is at most k, mid works: set hi = mid. Otherwise set lo = mid + 1.
pitfalls: Starting the search at sum / k or 0. A limit below the largest single value makes the greedy loop put a too-heavy value into a run on its own and report success wrongly.
Rejecting a limit because the greedy used fewer than k runs. Fewer runs is fine; a run can always be split.
Cutting greedily by trying to make every run close to sum / k without the search. The greedy only works for a fixed limit.

solutions.title: DP over prefix and run count
solutions.idea: best[j][i] is the lowest cost for the first i values in j runs; try every start of the last run.

solutions.title: Binary search on the limit
solutions.idea: A limit is achievable if greedy packing needs at most k runs. Search the smallest such limit between max and sum.

followups: Return the cut positions as well, not only the cost.
The values may be negative. Does the greedy check still work? Why not?
